Topological Field Theories and the Algebraic Structures
of the Two-Sphere
Chris Li
May 21, 2026
Abstract
We give two presentations for bordisms of S2 in the 3-dimensional oriented bor-
dism category Cob(3), encoding the algebraic structures on S2. After passing through
topological field theories, we define two kinds of monoids which we call P-monoids and
L-monoids. In addition to both being commutative Frobenius monoids, P-monoids are
equipped with a class of endomorphisms while L-monoids are equipped with a class
of unit morphisms, all of which are labelled by closed oriented irreducible prim

An n-dimensional topological field theory is a symmetric monoidal functor: Z : Cob(n) →Vectk . where Cob(n) is the category of closed oriented n-manifolds and cobordisms modulo orientation and boundary preserving diffeomorphisms, Vectk is the category of (insert your favorite adjectives here such as topological) k-vector spaces. Historically, this definition was given by [Ati88], possibly inspired by [Seg88]’s at- tempt to define a conformal field theory and [Wit82] on the relation between Morse theory and supersymmetry. Unpacking the definition, a topological field theory is a nice assignment

A fully-extended n-dimensional topological field theory is a sym- metric monoidal functor of (∞, n)-categories Z : Bordn →C. The (∞, n) category Bordn has objects 0-dimensional manifolds, 1-morphisms are cobordisms between 0-dimensional manifolds, 2-morphisms are cobordisms between cobordisms, etc. The n-morphisms can be interpreted as an n-dimensional manifold with corners. The (n + 1)-morphisms are diffeomorphisms between two n-manifold with corners, and the (n + 2)-morphisms are isotopies between diffeomorphisms, etc. This construction was proposed by [Lur08] and later corrected by [CS19] a

Consider the symmetric monoidal category Cob(3). It has a sub- category whose objects are disjoint unions of S2. Call this category Cob(3)S2 and note that it inherits the symmetric monoidal structure. In particular, the morphisms in Cob(3)S2 all have spherical boundaries. blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
Motivations
One of the greatest scientific achievements in the 20th century is the development
of quantum field theories, which model the interaction of elementary particles with
great precision through quantum fields. Quantum fields are , roughly speaking, classes
of functions ϕ : M →C where M is a manifold representing the underlying space-
time. Unfortunately, developing a mathematically rigorous definition of quantum field
theories has proven extremely challenging, leaving one of the most foundational subjects
of modern physics on unstable soil.
Topological field theories are toy models of

The 2-dimensional oriented bordism category Cob(2) is the free sym- metric monoidal category with a single commutative Frobenius algebra object. In par- ticular the category of oriented 2-dimensional topological field theories is equivalent to the category of commutative Frobenius algebras. This theorem was widely known and formal proofs appeared in numerous papers such as [Dij89], [Abr96], and J. [Koc03]. The category Cob(2) has objects closed oriented 1-dimensional manifolds (namely, a disjoint union of oriented circles), and morphisms are cobordisms between the disjoint unions of circles mo

Cob(3)S2 has a presentation with G2 generators under commutative Frobenius relations and legs relations. These relations are necessary. The G1 presentation is given by the usual commutative Frobenius relations only. We prove in theorem 4.3.2 that

Cob(3)S2 has a presentation with G1 generators and commutative Frobenius relations. What is perhaps surprising about the theorems is that the relations are extremely simple, even though the topology of 3-manifolds are significantly more complicated than the topology of 2-manifolds. In Cob(2) , a morphism is a 2-manifold with bound- aries. The classification of 2-manifolds shows that up to diffeomorphisms the manifold is classified by its genus. The classification of 3-manifolds is more complicated but standard– the theorem of Kneser-Milnor prime decomposition will play a repeated central role

There is a canonical isomorphism S : Cob(2) ∼ →Cob(3)S2,CF The isomorphism S sends n-copies of S1 to n-copies of S2, and sends the multi- plication map of S1 to the multiplication map of S2. Same goes for unit, trace, and co-multiplication. On more complicated bordisms, S sends a genus g bordism to a bor- dism with g-many S2 × S1 connect sum factors. This theorem essentially shows that the commutative Frobenius part of Cob(S2) is completely determined by Cob(2). \begin{defn} \label{defn:Trace of Surgery}
(Trace of Surgery) Let $M$ be an oriented $n$-manifold and $0\leq k\leq n$. Let $\phi : S^{k-1} \times D^{n-k} \hookrightarrow M$ be an embedding along which a $k$-handle is attached. The resulting manifold is \[
M' = M \cup_{\phi } (D^k \times D^{n-k})
.\]
The \textit{trace} of this handle attachment is the $(n+1)$-dimensional cobordism $W$ from $M$ to $M'$ obtained by attaching a $k$-handle to $M \times [0,1]$ along $M\times \left\{ 1 \right\} $: \[
W = (M \times [0,1]) \cup_{\phi } (D^k \times D^{n-k+1})
.\]

blocks.content: 1.1. (Free Category) Let G be a directed graph. The free category F(G) has objects the vertices of G and morphisms all composable arrows. The empty path is the identity of a vertex.

1.2. (Binary Relation) Let C be a category and a, b ∈obj(C). A bi- nary relation Ra,b on HomC(a, b) is a subset Ra,b ⊂HomC(a, b) × HomC(a, b). We write fRa,bg if (f, g) ∈Ra,b. We say R is a binary relation on homs of C if R = {Ra,b | a, b ∈obj(C)} is a collection of binary relations on all pairs of objects of C. If a pair of morphisms (f, f′) is in Ra,b, we write fRa,bf′, or f = f′ if the context is clear.

1.3. (Congruence) A congruence R on a category C is an assignment to each pair of objects a, b ∈obj(C) an equivalence relation Ra,b on HomC(a, b) that is compatible with compositions: if fRa,bf′, meaning if (f, f′) are equivalent, then for all g : a′ →a and all h : b →b′ one has (hfg)Ra′,b′(hf′g); if eRb,ce′, then (ef)Ra,c(e′f′). We sometimes write f ∼R f′ instead to denote the fact that R is a congruence rather than a binary relation.

1.6. (Quotient Category) Let C be a category and R a congruence on C. Then the quotient category C/R has the same objects as C and the morphisms HomC/R(a, b) = HomC(a, b)/Ra,b are those of C modulo the equivalence relation Ra,b. If R is a binary relation, the quotient category C/R is defined as C/R′ where R′ is the least congruence containing R.

1.8. (Generators and Relations) Let G be a directed graph and R a binary relation on F(G), the free category of G. Then we say F(G)/R has generators G and relations R. An isomorphism F(G)/R →C and ⟨G | R⟩form a presentation of C. We say the morphisms of C are generated by the edges of G and the objects by the vertices, and that the binary relation R is sufficient.

1.10. (Smaller Relations) Let R, R′ be binary relations on homs of F(G). We say R′ is smaller than R, denoted R′ ⊊R, if R′ a,b ⊆Ra,b for all pairs of objects a, b and there exists at least one pair of objects X, Y such that R′ X,Y ⊊RX,Y . In English, R′ is smaller than R if it can be obtained from R by removing some binary relations.

1.11. (Necessary Relations) Let H, G, R be a presentation of C. Let H : F(G) →C be the composition H ◦QR. We say R is necessary if for any R′ smaller than R, the unique functor H ′ : F(G)/ ∼R′→C, through which H factors as H = H ′ ◦QR′ is no longer an isomorphism.
1.5. (Least Congruence) Given any binary relations R on homs of C, there is a least congruence R′ on C with R ⊂R′.

1.7. (Universal Property of Quotient Category) [Mac94] Let C be a category with R a binary relation on the homs. Let C/R be the quotient category. Then the quotient functor Q = QR : C →C/R, which is identity on objects and sends a morphism to its equivalence class,1 satisfy the following universal property: If H : C →D is any functor such that fRa,bf′ implies Hf = Hf′ for all f and f′, then there exists a unique functor H′ : C/R →D with H′ ◦QR = H.
